Maladaptive Strategies.value: avoid anything that could be stressful
I tell myself the event did not really happen or was not that bad

Threat.value: Irritable behavior, angry outbursts, or acting aggressively
My body feels constantly tense and ready to react to danger
I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I try to explain what happened I lose the thread and cannot finish
I can taste what I tasted during the event when the memory returns

issues.item: Threat: Noticing Weapons: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
issues.explanation: For toxic chemical exposure, hypervigilance can be coherent, but specifically scanning for weapons or dangerous objects points to an interpersonal/assaultive threat context rather than chemical contamination. This threat item is hard to reconcile with the stated trauma type and with the memory items, which are sensory and exposure-based rather than assault-related.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Sexual Coping: I release my tension with sexual fantasies/ activities
issues.explanation: Sexual coping is not impossible, but here it is weakly anchored to the rest of the profile. The active formulation is dominated by Memory–Threat–Maladaptive Strategies links around re-experiencing and danger, while the other strategy items are broad avoidance/denial. This item addresses tension reduction in a way not otherwise represented by the triggers, threat, or memory content, making the profile less clinically coherent.

vignette:
Priya Krishnamurthy is a fifty-year-old South Asian woman, currently single, who has spent the better part of two decades representing her country's interests in multilateral diplomatic forums across the world. She presents for psychological assessment approximately fourteen months after a chemical exposure incident that occurred during a formal reception at a foreign consulate - an event she describes haltingly, and only in fragments, as though the story keeps slipping out of her grip before she can finish telling it.

The incident itself unfolded without warning. Priya was standing near a ventilation corridor, holding a glass of water and engaged in conversation with a colleague, when she became aware of a sharp, acrid taste - metallic and medicinal, coating the back of her throat almost before she had registered anything unusual in the air. Within minutes, others around her were coughing; there was confusion, then the controlled chaos of an evacuation. She was assessed at a field hospital and discharged, but three colleagues were hospitalised for several days. The investigation that followed was inconclusive in ways that have never fully satisfied her. What lodged most deeply was not the physical sensation of the exposure itself but the sudden, vertiginous understanding that the environment she had trusted - a diplomatic space, a room full of protocol and procedure - had been silently dangerous.

In the weeks following, Priya noticed that the memory did not behave like other difficult memories. It did not wait to be summoned. At a working lunch six weeks after the incident, she lifted a glass of mineral water and the faint mineral aftertaste triggered an immediate, total return of the experience - the metallic coating on her tongue, the sound of chairs scraping, the quality of the light in that corridor - arriving without transition, without warning, as though the intervening weeks had not existed. These intrusions, arriving through taste above all, left her shaken in ways she struggled to articulate. When asked by a colleague what had happened, she found she could not explain it; she would begin, lose the thread, and trail into silence. The memory, it seemed, was not stored in a form she could narrate.

It was partly to prevent these intrusions that Priya began, gradually and then systematically, to restructure her life. She stopped attending receptions that were not strictly mandatory. She avoided any setting where food or drink would be served in formal glassware. She began telling herself, with increasing insistence, that the event had not been as serious as it had seemed in the moment - that she had been unharmed, that the whole thing had been somewhat exaggerated in her mind. This minimisation offered brief relief, but it also meant she never fully processed what had happened, and the memory remained unintegrated, ready to surface. The avoidance and the magical thinking, rather than quieting the intrusions, seemed to keep the memory raw, so that when a trigger did break through her defences, the return was as vivid and destabilising as ever.

Her body, meanwhile, had arrived at its own conclusions. Priya now moves through her professional world - the conference rooms, the state dinners, the bilateral briefings that constitute a diplomat's daily life - in a state of sustained physiological alertness. She scans rooms when she enters them, noting ventilation points and exit routes before she has consciously decided to do so. Her jaw is frequently clenched. She has had two episodes of sharp, disproportionate anger with junior staff that she found mortifying and could not fully explain. This constant state of readiness feeds back into the memory system in a way she has not yet named but clearly experiences: when her body is already primed, the threshold for a full intrusive return drops, and the taste memory surfaces more readily. The hypervigilance and the intrusions sustain each other in a loop that has narrowed her world considerably over the past year.

What finally brought her to seek help was a formal diplomatic dinner three weeks ago at which she could not eat, could not concentrate on the conversation beside her, and left early with an excuse she knew was transparent. She is afraid, she says quietly, that she is becoming someone she does not recognise - and she is hoping, with characteristic precision, to understand what is happening to her.
